title: How Much? How Often?
theme: Quantity and frequency (shades of 'a lot' and 'a little')
objectives: I can use ten words to say how much and how often.
I can order amount and frequency words from least to most.
I can use context clues to choose the best word in a science text.
I can write about a place using precise words for amounts.
rationale: Amount and frequency words are the precision tools of informational writing: a student who can only say a lot, a little, or often cannot describe data or settings with accuracy. The ten words fall into three groups: enough or more, not enough or thin, and how often. Each ladder shows that these words are not interchangeable, and the desert passage gives them a concrete science context. Meager and sparse revisit the resource and decline ideas from unit 5.

words.def: More than enough; there is a large amount of it.
words.ex: Wild berries were plentiful along the trail, so the hikers ate their fill.
words.ex2: In spring, rain is plentiful and the creek runs high.
words.nonExample: A single crumb on a plate is not a plentiful meal.

apps.academic: In science, a plentiful resource is one that is not likely to run out soon.
apps.spoken: Good news: pencils are plentiful, so everyone can take two.
apps.writing: Use plentiful to show that there is more of something than anyone needs.

cloze.s: Apples were ___ in the orchard, and every basket was full by noon.

cloze2.s: Because fish were ___ in the bay, the boats came home loaded to the rails.

misuse.s: Water was plentiful in the dry valley, so the travelers worried about running out.
misuse.why: Plentiful means there is more than enough; worrying about running out shows the opposite.

visual.alt: Baskets overflowing with apples under a tree.

words.def: Very small in amount; not enough.
words.ex: The meager harvest left the family with only a few sacks of grain.
words.ex2: She earned a meager wage, so every coin mattered.
words.nonExample: A table piled high with food is not a meager meal.

apps.academic: Historians write about meager harvests that caused hunger in a village.
apps.spoken: My lunch was meager today, so I am still hungry.
apps.writing: Use meager to describe a portion or pay that is smaller than people need.

cloze.s: After the long drought, the farmers brought in only a ___ crop of corn.

cloze2.s: The ___ dinner of one thin slice of bread did not fill him up.

misuse.s: The feast was meager, with tables overflowing with roasted food.
misuse.why: Meager means very small in amount; tables overflowing show a large amount.

visual.alt: A large plate holding one small slice of bread.

words.frame: A meager meal is one that ___.

words.def: Enough, with some left over; roomy.
words.ex: Our new library has ample shelf space for thousands more books.
words.ex2: Dad allowed ample time for the drive, so we arrived early.
words.nonExample: Two minutes is not ample time to finish a long test.

apps.academic: A fair test gives students ample time to think through each problem.
apps.spoken: We have ample room in the van, so bring your friend along.
apps.writing: Use ample for space, time, or supplies that are more than enough.

cloze.s: The backpack had ___ room for lunch, a water bottle, and two thick books.

cloze2.s: With ___ time before the bell, Sam checked each answer twice.

misuse.s: The closet was ample, so we could not fit even one more coat inside.
misuse.why: Ample means more than enough room; no room left shows the opposite.

visual.alt: A big open backpack with plenty of space around the books.

words.def: Thinly spread, with big gaps between things.
words.ex: Grass was sparse on the rocky hill, with bare dirt showing between the tufts.
words.ex2: Sparse crowds came to the game because of the heavy rain.
words.nonExample: A thick forest where the trees touch is not sparse.

apps.academic: On the map, the dots are sparse in the north, so few people live there.
apps.spoken: The room was pretty sparse, with just one chair and a lamp.
apps.writing: Use sparse to show that things are far apart or few in number.

cloze.s: Only a few ___ trees grew on the desert plain, far apart from one another.

cloze2.s: The audience was ___, and whole rows of seats sat empty.

misuse.s: The sparse forest was so crowded that we could barely squeeze between the trees.
misuse.why: Sparse means thinly spread; a crowded forest is the opposite.

visual.alt: A few cactuses far apart on a wide, sandy desert.

words.def: So many that you cannot number them all.
words.ex: Countless stars filled the sky above the quiet campsite.
words.ex2: Countless raindrops tapped the roof all night long.
words.nonExample: Three pencils on a desk are not countless.

morph.note: Countless means "without a count," so it names an amount too large to count.

apps.academic: Scientists say there are countless tiny living things in a spoonful of soil.
apps.spoken: I have asked you countless times to close the gate!
apps.writing: Use countless to show a number so big that counting would never finish.

cloze.s: Beach visitors left ___ footprints in the sand, too many for anyone to tally.

cloze2.s: The night sky held ___ stars, more than the campers could ever number.

misuse.s: There were countless seats in the tiny room, exactly four, and we counted them all.
misuse.why: Countless means too many to count; four seats are easy to count.

visual.alt: A night sky packed with stars above a small tent.

words.def: Happening now and then, not often.
words.ex: We had occasional showers this week, but most days stayed sunny.
words.ex2: Grandpa takes an occasional walk to the lake when his knees feel good.
words.nonExample: A bell that rings every hour is not occasional.

apps.academic: An occasional error in a data table is normal; a pattern of errors is a problem.
apps.spoken: I like an occasional pizza night, but not every week.
apps.writing: Use occasional for events that come now and then without a set pattern.

cloze.s: She is an ___ visitor who stops by maybe twice a year.

cloze2.s: The ___ drop of rain hit the window, but the storm never really came.

misuse.s: He is an occasional runner who jogs every single morning without fail.
misuse.why: Occasional means now and then; jogging every morning is regular.

visual.alt: A mostly sunny sky with one small rain cloud.

words.frame: An occasional treat for me is ___.

words.ex: Frequent storms in spring flooded the low road several times.
words.ex2: The bus makes frequent stops, so the ride takes longer.
words.nonExample: A holiday that comes once a year is not a frequent event.

apps.academic: Frequent measurements of the plant helped the class see how fast it grew.
apps.spoken: I send frequent messages to my cousin overseas.
apps.writing: Use frequent to show that something happens many times, not just once.

cloze.s: Because of ___ rain, the soccer field was muddy every afternoon this week.

cloze2.s: Mia is a ___ visitor at the library, and the librarian knows her by name.

misuse.s: A leap day is a frequent event that happens almost every week.
misuse.why: Frequent means happening often; a leap day comes about once every four years.

visual.alt: Rain clouds with a circular arrow showing it happens again and again.

words.frame: A frequent ___ in my life is ___.

words.def: Happening over and over, with short breaks.
words.ex: The continual ringing of the phone forced her to leave the room.
words.ex2: Waves cause continual changes to the shape of the beach.
words.nonExample: A light that stays on all day without blinking is continuous, not continual.

morph.note: The final e of continue is dropped before -al.

apps.academic: Continual practice helps scientists get steady results in an experiment.
apps.spoken: The continual noise outside made it hard to focus.
apps.writing: Use continual for something that keeps coming back again and again.

cloze.s: Her ___ interruptions, one every minute, kept the speaker from finishing a sentence.

cloze2.s: The ___ tapping of the leaky faucet, drip after drip, kept Ben awake.

misuse.s: The continual noise happened one time and never came back all year.
misuse.why: Continual means happening again and again; a one-time noise is not continual.

visual.alt: A faucet with water dripping again and again into a sink.

words.frame: A continual sound in my home is ___.

words.ex: Snow rarely falls in the southern town, so children there are thrilled when it does.
words.ex2: My cat rarely comes when I call, but she always runs for treats.
words.nonExample: A person who brushes twice a day does not rarely brush.

apps.academic: Scientists note when an event happens often and when it happens rarely.
apps.spoken: I rarely stay up late on school nights.
apps.writing: Use rarely to tell how seldom something happens.

cloze.s: The museum is ___ crowded on weekdays, so you can often walk right up to the exhibits.

cloze2.s: Sloths ___ come down from the trees; they do most things hanging from branches.

misuse.s: She rarely forgets her lunch, so she forgets it every single day.
misuse.why: Rarely means hardly ever; forgetting every day is the opposite.

visual.alt: A line from always through often and sometimes to rarely and never, with rarely near the never end.

words.def: As much as is needed; enough.
words.ex: Two cups of flour are sufficient for one batch of muffins.
words.ex2: Do we have sufficient evidence to say the plant needs more light?
words.nonExample: One cracker is not sufficient for a hungry hiker after a long climb.

apps.academic: A scientist needs sufficient data before drawing a conclusion.
apps.spoken: Is one sandwich sufficient for you, or do you want two?
apps.writing: Use sufficient when something meets a need but is not more than the need.

cloze.s: With ___ water in the jug for one day, the campers did not need to refill it.

cloze2.s: Mr. Ortiz said one clear example was ___, so we stopped writing more.

misuse.s: Three drops of water are sufficient to fill a large bathtub.
misuse.why: Sufficient means enough for the need; three drops cannot fill a bathtub.

passage.title: Life on Dry Ground
paras: A desert is a place that gets very little rain. In many deserts, the yearly rainfall is meager, often less than ten inches. Rain seldom falls, and months can pass without a single drop. Because the ground stays dry, plants are sparse. Instead of covering the land, they grow far apart, with bare sand between them.

Still, the desert is not empty. Sunshine is plentiful, and living things have found clever ways to survive. After an occasional storm, a saguaro cactus soaks up water through its shallow roots and stores it inside its thick trunk. A large saguaro can hold ample water to last through many dry months.

Animals face a continual search for water. The kangaroo rat has a surprising answer. It rarely, if ever, takes a drink. The seeds it eats give it sufficient water for its small body. It also hides in a cool burrow during the hot day and comes out at night.

At night, the desert changes. The air cools, and countless stars shine in a sky with no city lights. Frequent winds push the sand into long, curving hills called dunes, so the land slowly changes shape. The desert may look still, but it is full of life.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "meager" most nearly means
qs.why: The paragraph says rain is less than ten inches a year and months pass with no drop, so meager means a very small amount.

qs.q: What does the author mean by saying that desert plants are sparse?
choices: They grow in thick patches near each other.
They only live for one season.
They are too small for animals to eat.
They grow far apart with bare ground between them.
qs.why: The next sentence explains that the plants grow far apart with bare sand between them.

qs.q: Which detail best shows how a saguaro cactus survives long dry spells?
choices: It stores water in its thick trunk after a storm.
It lives where sunshine is plentiful.
It has shallow roots that sit near rocks.
qs.why: The text says the saguaro soaks up water and stores it in its trunk to last through many dry months.

qs.q: Why can the kangaroo rat live without taking many drinks?
choices: It hides in a burrow all year.
Its seeds give it enough water.
qs.why: The text says the seeds it eats give it sufficient water, so it rarely needs to drink.

qs.q: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Deserts are always too hot for plants.
Plants and animals in the desert find clever ways to live with very little water.
Kangaroo rats are the most important desert animals.
Winds and dunes are the main thing that makes deserts.
qs.why: Each paragraph shows a living thing or place using a clever way to live with little water.

argue.prompt: Claim: A school should give students ample time for tests, even if the school day becomes longer. Take a side and give two reasons using words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. Having ample time means ___.

constructed.prompt: Describe two places, one where food is plentiful and one where food is meager. Use both words and show what you would see in each place.
look: gives a concrete detail for each
constructed.model: At the farmers' market, fruit is plentiful: tables are stacked high with peaches and melons. In the village after the drought, food was meager: each family got only a small cup of rice.

constructed.prompt: Write about three events in your week, one that happens rarely, one that is frequent, and one that is continual. Use all three words and explain how you decided.
look: gives a different event for each
constructed.model: I rarely go to the dentist, just twice a year. Math homework is frequent, since I have it most nights. The continual sound of a clock ticking in our kitchen happens over and over all day.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for how much and how often, order them on two ladders, read an informational passage about desert life, and write about amounts and frequency. The unit gives writers precise alternatives to a lot, a little, and often.

notes.va.plentiful.adj: Plentiful and ample overlap. Use plentiful for a large supply and ample for enough room or time, with some left over. Have students sort real examples into two columns.
notes.va.meager.adj: Meager is about smallness of an amount, and it often has a feeling of worry about it. Link to frugal and stingy from unit 5: meager is what a person has, while frugal is how a person spends.
notes.va.ample.adj: Ample is a positive word. Students may think it means big; clarify that an ample space is large enough for the need. Practice with room, time, and supplies.
notes.va.sparse.adj: Sparse describes things spread thinly, such as trees, crowds, or hair, not an amount in a container. Show two dot maps, one dense and one sparse.
notes.va.countless.adj: Countless is a figure of speech here, not a literal claim. Ask whether stars are countless in a city and in a desert, and why the answer changes.
notes.va.occasional.adj: Occasional means now and then and has no pattern. Contrast it on a calendar with regular, such as every Monday.
notes.va.frequent.adj: Frequent is the one that happens many times. Ask students to put tallies on a chart to make frequent visible.
notes.va.continual.adj: Continual is repeated, with breaks, while continuous has no break. Many speakers use them as one word, so tell students the difference matters mostly in careful science and formal writing. Use a dripping faucet for continual and a flowing river for continuous.
notes.va.rarely.adv: Rarely is an adverb that modifies a verb. Students often place it incorrectly, so model I rarely walk and not I walk rarely, and point out that both can work.
notes.va.sufficient.adj: Sufficient means exactly enough for a need. Pair it with a measuring cup, a recipe, or an experiment to show that enough is relative to the job.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The passage says rainfall is less than ten inches a year and months pass without a drop. That is not enough for most plants, so meager fits. It also says the kangaroo rat rarely drinks, which means hardly ever. I can check each word against a detail in the text.'
discuss: Is a large amount always a good thing? Use plentiful or ample in your answer.
Which words from the unit would a scientist use to describe a rainforest, and which would describe a desert?
misconceptions: Continual and continuous always mean the same thing.
extend: Make a how-much ladder with five new words from a thesaurus and defend the order.
Write a short paragraph for a science report about a place using at least four words from the unit.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit frugal, stingy, and dwindle in a sentence with a unit word, such as a meager budget that forced a frugal choice. Return to the two ladders after two days, again at one week, and use them in science writing.

There is sufficient ___ for ___, so we do not need ___.
wida.oral: Partner A names a place and one thing there that is plentiful or meager without saying the word; Partner B says the matching word and finishes the sentence frame.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (escaso, ample/amplio, incontable, frecuente, continuo) not reviewed by a native speaker; escaso is used for both meager and sparse.
Sense boundary of continual versus continuous: many dictionaries treat them as near-synonyms in everyday use; the unit teaches the careful-writing distinction.
Desert facts (rainfall under ten inches in many deserts, saguaro water storage, kangaroo rats getting water from seeds) are standard but have not been checked against a cited source.
